newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila, APEC allies join hands to protect leaders.
newsitem.headline: Manila, APEC allies join hands to protect leaders.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos said on Wednesday the Philippines was working closely with Asia-Pacific governments to neutralise any security threats to leaders attending next month's APEC summit.
"These (consultations) have been going on for a long time ... so that there will be no security threats and if there are any, that that (they) will be prevented, preempted," he said.

Ramos also said his government stood firm on its decision to bar the entry of Nobel peace laureate Jose Ramos-Horta during the November 25 summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
He stressed, however, that Ramos-Horta was being kept out of the country not because he was a security threat but because his presence in the country "is inimical to our national interests."

The East Timorese resistance leader has been invited by Filipino peace activists to speak on the issue of Indonesia's occupation of the former Portuguese colony at a meeting of international non-governmental organisations to be held in parallel with the APEC summit.
Indonesian President Suharto is one of the leaders expected to attend the APEC summit.
"That's our position. It has not changed," Ramos told his weekly news conference, referring to the ban on Ramos-Horta.

Ramos said the close coordination that had been going on among APEC members' security agencies was normal in international conferences, especially those in which not only senior ministers but leaders themselves were attending.
"(We) have networked already, coordinated, exchanged information, arrangements, even equipment," he said.

Ramos did not say if there were specific threats to any APEC leader. Philippine security officials earlier said they considered U.S. President Bill Clinton, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Suharto as the "top risks".
Eighteen bullet-proof Mercedez Benzes bought from Germany arrived on Wednesday for use by the APEC leaders. The vehicles arrived with 18 Mercedes look-alikes to serve as decoys.

"From here on, nobody touches them ... We are watching (them) like a hawk," former armed forces chief Lisandro Abadia, head of a committee supervising APEC preparations, told reporters after inspecting the vehicles which the government has leased for 9.8 million pesos ($376,000).
"We cannot leave anything to chance for our guests," he said.

Ramos said the international coordination to ensure the security of the APEC summit was similar to consultations Manila had with foreign security agencies when Pope John Paul visited the country in January 1995.
Days before the Pope arrived, local police uncovered a plot by Islamic extremists to bomb U.S. aircraft flying between Asia and the U.S. mainland.
The discovery of the plot later led to the arrest of Ramzi Ahmed Yousef and his eventual trial and conviction in the United States for which President Clinton thanked Manila, Ramos said.
An angry Ramos earlier on Wednesday ordered police to stop demolishing squatter huts near the presidential palace after a violent scuffle erupted between squatters and demolition workers.
The destruction of squatter huts had been ordered by local mayors as part of a campaign to beautify Manila ahead of the summit.
Ramos was meeting with a group of slum dwellers to discuss relocation plans when wrecking crews began tearing down 300 shanties, sparking scuffles in which 15 people were injured.
